cse-1996-a-53.approach: Feed the two control lines to the select inputs of a 4-to-1 MUX; then each data input only has to produce one fixed function of A and B, and the four gates supplied make exactly those four functions.

steps.title: Use $C_1C_0$ as the select inputs
steps.body:
With $S_1=C_1$, $S_0=C_0$ the MUX passes $I_{2C_1+C_0}$ to the output:

| $C_1C_0$ | input routed | must equal |
|---|---|---|
| 00 | $I_0$ | $\overline{A+B}$ |
| 01 | $I_1$ | $A+B$ |
| 10 | $I_2$ | $A\oplus B$ |
| 11 | $I_3$ | $AB$ |

steps.title: Build the data inputs
steps.body:
- OR gate: $A+B \to I_1$.
- Inverter on the OR output: $\overline{A+B} \to I_0$ (this is why only one OR gate is needed).
- XOR gate: $A\oplus B \to I_2$.
- AND gate: $AB \to I_3$.

Every listed component is used exactly once.

steps.title: Check the output
steps.body: $F=\overline{C_1}\,\overline{C_0}\,\overline{A+B}+\overline{C_1}C_0(A+B)+C_1\overline{C_0}(A\oplus B)+C_1C_0\,AB$, which is the given table row by row.

answer.value: 4-to-1 MUX with $S_1=C_1$, $S_0=C_0$; $I_0=\overline{A+B}$ (OR gate followed by the inverter), $I_1=A+B$ (OR output), $I_2=A\oplus B$ (XOR), $I_3=AB$ (AND); the MUX output is F.

pitfalls: Swapping $S_1$/$S_0$ routes $A+B$ and $A\oplus B$ to the wrong rows.
Do not use a second OR gate for $\overline{A+B}$: invert the one OR output.
cse-1996-a-53.verification: Substituted each control combination into the MUX equation and got the table entry.

cse-1996-a-54.approach: Assemble the program to find addresses: PCHL jumps to the address in HL = 0105H, which is the OUT instruction, so OUT–INR–PCHL is an endless loop that writes an incrementing accumulator to the port.
cse-1996-a-54.given:
| Address | Instruction | Bytes |
|---|---|---|
| 0100H | MVI A, 00H | 2 |
| 0102H | LXI H, 0105H | 3 |
| 0105H | OUT 00H | 2 |
| 0107H | INR A | 1 |
| 0108H | PCHL | 1 |
| 0109H | HLT | 1 |

steps.title: Locate the jump target
steps.body: MVI takes 2 bytes (0100H–0101H) and LXI 3 bytes (0102H–0104H), so OUT 00H starts at 0105H. LXI loads HL = 0105H, and PCHL copies HL into PC, so control goes back to OUT. HLT is never reached.

steps.title: What the port sees
steps.body: Each pass outputs A and then increments it: the port shows 00H, 01H, 02H, …, FFH, 00H, … forever. Port 00H works as an 8-bit binary up-counter (the processor never halts).

steps.title: Loop timing
steps.body: T-states per pass: OUT = 10, INR A = 4, PCHL = 6, so $10+4+6=20$ T-states. A new value appears every 20 T-states.

steps.title: Waveforms of the three LSBs
steps.body:
- $D_0$ toggles every pass: square wave, period $2\times20=40$ T.
- $D_1$ toggles every 2 passes: period $80$ T.
- $D_2$ toggles every 4 passes: period $160$ T.

Each bit is a 50 % duty-cycle square wave with twice the period of the bit below it ($D_0$ at $f$, $D_1$ at $f/2$, $D_2$ at $f/4$), all changing only at the OUT instants.

answer.value: (a) It loops OUT 00H → INR A → PCHL (back to 0105H) forever, so port 00H counts 00H, 01H, …, FFH, 00H, … — an 8-bit binary counter. (b) Bits $D_0$, $D_1$, $D_2$ are square waves with periods 40, 80 and 160 T-states (each half the frequency of the previous).

pitfalls: PCHL jumps to 0105H (OUT), not to 0100H — A is not reset to 00H.
The program never reaches HLT.
cse-1996-a-54.verification: Recounted instruction lengths: 2 + 3 = 5 bytes after 0100H gives 0105H for OUT.

cse-1996-a-55.approach: Page size 256 B means the page number is the high byte of the 16-bit address; 1 KB of memory holds 4 frames. Run LRU on the four references starting from the given list (three pages loaded, one free frame).
concepts: Address split into page and offset
cse-1996-a-55.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Page size | $256=2^8$ B (low byte = offset) |
| Frames | $1024/256=4$ |
| LRU list (LRU → MRU) | 17, 1, 63 |

steps.title: Page numbers
steps.body: Take the high byte: 00FF → page $00H=0$; 010D → page $01H=1$; 10FF → page $10H=16$; 11B0 → page $11H=17$.

scene.caption: Initial state: 17, 1, 63 resident (LRU on the left); one frame free.

steps.title: 00FF → page 0
steps.body: Page 0 is not resident: **page fault**. A frame is still free, so **no replacement**. List: [17, 1, 63, 0].

scene.caption: Page 0: fault, loaded into the free frame.

steps.title: 010D → page 1
steps.body: Page 1 is resident: **hit**, move it to the MRU end. List: [17, 63, 0, 1].

scene.caption: Page 1: hit, becomes most recently used.

steps.title: 10FF → page 16
steps.body: Not resident: **page fault**; memory is full, so **replace the LRU page 17**. List: [63, 0, 1, 16].

steps.title: 11B0 → page 17
steps.body: Page 17 was just evicted: **page fault**, **replace the LRU page 63**. List: [0, 1, 16, 17].

animation.title: LRU with 4 frames (first 3 refs rebuild the given list)

answer.value: 00FF (page 0): fault, no replacement → [17, 1, 63, 0]; 010D (page 1): hit → [17, 63, 0, 1]; 10FF (page 16): fault, replaces 17 → [63, 0, 1, 16]; 11B0 (page 17): fault, replaces 63 → [0, 1, 16, 17]. Three faults, two replacements.

pitfalls: Memory has 4 frames, not 3 — the first fault needs no replacement.
Page numbers are hexadecimal high bytes: 10H = 16 and 11H = 17, not 10 and 11.
cse-1996-a-55.verification: The animation preloads 17, 1, 63 (3 faults) and then shows exactly 3 more faults for the four given addresses: 6 in total.

cse-1996-b-56.approach: Two functions are equivalent exactly when they agree at 3, so a class is fixed by the value $f(3)$; the values at 1 and 2 are free.

steps.title: Number of classes
steps.body: $f(3)$ can be 1, 2 or 3, and each value is taken by some function, so there are **3** equivalence classes.

steps.title: Size of each class
steps.body: Fix $f(3)=c$. Then $f(1)$ and $f(2)$ are each any of 3 values: $3\times3=9$ functions per class.

answer.value: (a) 3 equivalence classes; (b) 9 functions in each class.

cse-1996-b-57.approach: Prove $P(k)$: "$f_{3k}$ is even" by induction on $k$, using the recurrence twice to write $f_{3k+3}$ in terms of $f_{3k}$ and an even term.

steps.title: Base case
steps.body: $f_3=f_2+f_1=1+1=2$, which is even, so $P(1)$ holds.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body: Assume $f_{3k}$ is even. $2f_{3k+1}$ is even, and the sum of two even numbers is even, so $f_{3k+3}$ is even. Hence $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)$, and by induction $f_3,f_6,f_9,\ldots$ are all even.

answer.value: Base: $f_3=2$ is even. Step: $f_{3k+3}=f_{3k+2}+f_{3k+1}=2f_{3k+1}+f_{3k}$, so if $f_{3k}$ is even then $f_{3k+3}$ is even. Hence every third term $f_{3k}$ is even.

pitfalls: The question asks for an induction proof about parity, not a closed form such as Binet's formula.

steps.title: Invert M
steps.body: $\det M=1\cdot1-0\cdot1=1$, so $M^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: $$D=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}b_{11}&b_{12}\\b_{21}&b_{22}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}b_{11}&b_{12}\\b_{21}-b_{11}&b_{22}-b_{12}\end{bmatrix}$$

pitfalls: $(AM)^{-1}=M^{-1}A^{-1}$, not $A^{-1}M^{-1}$ — the order reverses.

cse-1996-b-59.approach: A and B are nullable, C is not. Replace $S\to ABAC$ by every version with some nullable symbols dropped, delete the ε-rules, then remove the unit rule $S\to C$ that appears.

steps.title: Nullable symbols
steps.body: $A\to\varepsilon$ and $B\to\varepsilon$, so A and B are nullable. C and S are not (C must derive d).

steps.title: Expand $S	o ABAC$
steps.body:
Drop any subset of the three nullable positions $A_1,B,A_2$:
- none: $ABAC$
- $A_1$: $BAC$; $B$: $AAC$; $A_2$: $ABC$
- $A_1,B$ or $B,A_2$: $AC$; $A_1,A_2$: $BC$
- all three: $C$

Then $A\to aA\mid a$, $B\to bB\mid b$.

steps.title: Remove the unit production
steps.body: $S\to C$ is a unit production; replace it by C's right side: $S\to d$.

steps.title: Result G'
steps.body:
$$\begin{aligned}S&\to ABAC\mid BAC\mid AAC\mid ABC\mid AC\mid BC\mid d\\A&\to aA\mid a\\B&\to bB\mid b\\C&\to d\end{aligned}$$
$\varepsilon\notin L(G)$ (every string ends in d), so no $S\to\varepsilon$ is needed.

answer.value: $S\to ABAC\mid BAC\mid AAC\mid ABC\mid AC\mid BC\mid d$; $A\to aA\mid a$; $B\to bB\mid b$; $C\to d$.

pitfalls: Removing ε-rules creates the unit rule $S\to C$; it must be replaced by $S\to d$.
Dropping $A_1,B$ and dropping $B,A_2$ both give $AC$ — list it once.
cse-1996-b-59.verification: $L(G)=a^*b^*a^*d$; G' generates the same strings, e.g. $d$ via $S\to d$ and $ad$ via $S\to AC$.

cse-1996-b-60.approach: Concatenation: ε-move from every final state of $M_1$ to the start of $M_2$ and make $M_1$'s finals non-final. Star: add ε-moves from $M_2$'s final states back to $M_1$'s start. Because $\varepsilon\in L_1L_2$ already, no new start state is needed.
cse-1996-b-60.given:
| Machine | States | Language |
|---|---|---|
| $M_1$ | A (start, final), B; A↔B on 0 and 1 | even-length strings over {0,1} |
| $M_2$ | C (start, final), D (final), E (dead) | $a^*b^*$ |

steps.title: Part (a): $L_1L_2$
steps.body:
Add $A\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}C$ (A is $M_1$'s only final state). Start state: A. Make A **non-final**; final states: C and D. B and E unchanged.

Any accepting path reads an $M_1$ string ending in A (even length), takes ε to C, and then reads an $a^*b^*$ word ending in C or D.

steps.title: Part (b): $(L_1L_2)^*$
steps.body: To the machine of (a), add $C\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A$ and $D\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A$. Start A, finals C and D (A stays non-final).

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body:
- An accepting path splits at the ε-moves into blocks: (path A→A in $M_1$) ε (path C→C/D in $M_2$) ε back to A … so it spells a word of $(L_1L_2)^+$.
- Every word of $(L_1L_2)^+$ has such a path.
- $\varepsilon$: $A\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}C$ with C final, so ε is accepted. Since $\varepsilon\in L_1L_2$, $(L_1L_2)^+=(L_1L_2)^*$.
- A is never made final, so the usual trap (start state with incoming edges made final) does not occur: B→A edges cannot end a string in an accepting state.

answer.value: (a) Add ε: A→C; start A; A becomes non-final; final states C and D. (b) Additionally add ε: C→A and D→A (finals still C and D); ε is accepted through A→C, so the machine accepts $(L_1L_2)^*$.

pitfalls: Keeping A final in (a) happens to be harmless here (ε ∈ L₂, so L₁ ⊆ L₁L₂), but the general construction makes the finals of $M_1$ non-final.
Do not add ε from E — it is not a final state.
cse-1996-b-60.verification: Trace "01ab": A–0→B–1→A, ε→C, a→C, b→D (final) ✓. "0" stays in B and is rejected ✓.

cse-1996-b-61.approach: An even palindrome $ww^R$ is accepted by pushing the first half and popping on matches. On reading a symbol equal to the top, the PDA must nondeterministically either keep pushing (still in the first half) or guess the middle and start matching in $q_2$.

steps.title: Roles of the states
steps.body: $q_1$: reading $w$, pushing each symbol (rules 1, 2). $q_2$: reading $w^R$, popping matching symbols (5, 6), and emptying the stack at Z (7).

steps.title: Rule (3): $delta(q_1,a,a)$
steps.body: Top is a and input is a. Either we are still in the first half: push, giving $(q_1, aa)$; or this a is the first symbol of the second half matching the last pushed a: pop and switch, $(q_2,\varepsilon)$.

steps.title: Rule (4): $delta(q_1,b,b)$
steps.body: Same idea: $(q_1, bb)$ or $(q_2,\varepsilon)$.

steps.title: Trace "aaaa"
steps.body: $q_1,Z \xrightarrow{a\,(1)} Za \xrightarrow{a\,(3)\text{ push}} Zaa \xrightarrow{a\,(3)\text{ guess middle}} Za$ in $q_2$ $\xrightarrow{a\,(5)} Z \xrightarrow{\varepsilon\,(7)}$ empty stack ✓.

answer.value: (3) $\delta(q_1,a,a)=\{(q_1,aa),(q_2,\varepsilon)\}$; (4) $\delta(q_1,b,b)=\{(q_1,bb),(q_2,\varepsilon)\}$.

pitfalls: Top of stack is at the right: pushing a on a gives "aa", popping gives ε.
The specification as printed lacks push moves for $\delta(q_1,a,b)$ and $\delta(q_1,b,a)$ (e.g. $(q_1,ba)$, $(q_1,ab)$); without them "abba" is rejected.
cse-1996-b-61.verification: "aa": push a, then (3) second option pops to Z in $q_2$, rule 7 empties the stack ✓.

cse-1996-b-62.approach: The array is a Young tableau: rows and columns increase, so the minimum is $A[1][1]$. Insertion from the top-left corner is a "sift-down": while x is bigger than a right or lower neighbour, move the smaller neighbour up/left into the hole and follow it.

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: Every element is larger than its left and upper neighbours, so following them back always reaches $A[1][1]$: the smallest item is at $i=1$, $j=1$.

steps.title: Loop condition (line 2)
steps.body: Keep moving while x is out of order with a neighbour: x > A[i+1][j] **or** x > A[i][j+1].

steps.title: Which neighbour moves (lines 3, 7)
steps.body:
Move the **smaller** neighbour into the hole so it stays smaller than the other one:
- line 3: if A[i+1][j] < A[i][j+1] then move down (lines 4–5);
- line 7 (else): A[i][j] := A[i][j+1]; j := j+1.

The printed line 3 compares with A[i][j]; it must compare the two neighbours, A[i][j+1].

steps.title: Place x (line 9) and cost
steps.body: When neither neighbour is smaller, A[i][j] := x. Each pass increases i or j, so at most $2n-2$ passes: $O(n)$. The guarantee that x is smaller than the last row/column keeps i, j < n inside the loop.

answer.value: (a) i = 1, j = 1. (b) line 2: x > A[i+1][j] or x > A[i][j+1]; line 3: if A[i+1][j] < A[i][j+1] then; line 7: A[i][j] := A[i][j+1]; j := j+1; line 9: A[i][j] := x.

pitfalls: Moving the larger neighbour breaks the order with the other neighbour.
Line 9 writes x, not a neighbour.
cse-1996-b-62.verification: Tableau rows (1,3),(2,5) with 1 deleted and x = 4: the smaller neighbour 2 moves up, i = 2; then 5 > 4 so stop and write 4: rows (2,3),(4,5) — still sorted.

cse-1996-b-63.approach: Map each letter to its alphabet position (a = 1, …), reduce mod 10, and probe forward on collisions. Only the last two keys find their home slot occupied.

steps.title: First eight keys
steps.body: K→1, R→8, P→6, C→3, S→9, N→4, Y→5, T→0: all home slots are empty, no collisions.

scene.caption: After K R P C S N Y T — no collisions.

steps.title: Insert J
steps.body: $h(J)=10 \bmod 10=0$: slot 0 (T) busy → **collision**; slot 1 (K) busy; slot 2 free → J at 2.

steps.title: Insert M
steps.body: $h(M)=13 \bmod 10=3$: slots 3 (C), 4 (N), 5 (Y), 6 (P) busy → **collision**; slot 7 free → M at 7.

scene.caption: M: probes 3–6, lands in 7. Table full.

answer.value: (a) Only J and M cause collisions. (b) 0: T, 1: K, 2: J, 3: C, 4: N, 5: Y, 6: P, 7: M, 8: R, 9: S.

pitfalls: Use the alphabet position (ord(x) − ord(a) + 1), so K = 11 → slot 1, not 10.
cse-1996-b-63.verification: Ten distinct keys fill all ten slots; every non-home placement (J, M) is the first free slot after its home.

cse-1996-b-64.approach: Use the cut property: an edge that is the unique lightest edge across some cut is in every MST. For |u−v| the weight-1 edges already form a spanning tree; for u+v, edge (0, v) is the lightest edge at every vertex v.

steps.title: (a) weight |u − v|
steps.body: Every edge weighs at least 1, and the $n-1$ edges of weight 1 are $(0,1),(1,2),\ldots,(n-2,n-1)$, which form a path through all vertices. A spanning tree has $n-1$ edges, so weight $\ge n-1$; the path achieves it. MST = **path** $0-1-2-\cdots-(n-1)$, weight $n-1$.

steps.title: (b) weight u + v
steps.body: For a vertex $v\ge1$, its edges weigh $v+u$; the lightest is $(0,v)$ with weight $v$ (unique). By the cut property on the cut $\{v\}$ vs. the rest, $(0,v)$ is in every MST. These $n-1$ edges already form a spanning tree: the **star** centred at 0.

answer.value: (a) The path $0-1-2-\cdots-(n-1)$ (weight $n-1$). (b) The star with centre 0: edges $(0,v)$ for $v=1,\ldots,n-1$ (weight $n(n-1)/2$).

pitfalls: In (b) a path 0–1–2–… costs $1+3+5+\cdots$, more than the star.
cse-1996-b-64.verification: n = 4, (b): star 1 + 2 + 3 = 6; any tree must contain each edge (0, v) by the cut argument, so 6 is optimal.

cse-1996-b-65.approach: Run Dijkstra from A, always finalising the closest unfinished vertex and relaxing its out-edges. (Several weights in the scanned figure are illegible; the run uses the readable weights 6, 41, 12, 10, 15, 22, 12, 90, 70 and assumes the unreadable A→E, C→E and F→D edges are not shortcuts.)

steps.title: Finalise C (59)
steps.body: Relax C→F: $59+10=69<70$, so $d(F)=69$. C→B gives $71>6$, no change.

steps.title: Finalise F (69), then E (84)
steps.body:
Relax F→E: $d(E)=69+15=84$. F→B, F→D give nothing better. Finally E is finalised with 84.

Order identified: **A, B, D, C, F, E**. Path (follow predecessors back from E): $A\to B\to D\to C\to F\to E$, cost $6+41+12+10+15=84$.

animation.caption: Dashed edges: weights illegible in the scan.

answer.value: (a) A, B, D, C, F, E; (b) A → B → D → C → F → E; (c) 84.

pitfalls: A→C (90) and A→F (70) are direct but longer than the detour through B and D.
cse-1996-b-65.verification: $6+41=47$, $47+12=59$, $59+10=69$, $69+15=84$; every finalised distance is at most every tentative one when it is chosen.

cse-1996-b-66.approach: Look for a range where the loop makes no progress. Because the update is i := k (not k+1) and k = (i+j) div 2, a two-element range j = i+1 gives k = i, and if a[i] < x then i stays i forever.

steps.title: Find the stuck state
steps.body: If $j=i+1$ then $k=\lfloor(2i+1)/2\rfloor=i$. If $a[i]<x$: i := k = i, nothing changes, $a[k]\ne x$ and $i<j$, so the **loop never ends**. (If $a[i]\ge x$, j := i and the loop stops.)

steps.title: When is that state reached?
steps.body: The updates keep the invariant "if x is present it is in a[i..j]" and, once $a[1]<x$, also $a[i]<x$. So if $x>a[1]$ and x is never hit exactly at a probe k, the range shrinks to $j=i+1$ with $a[i]<x$ and the program hangs.

steps.title: Failing cases
When it works
steps.body: If $x\le a[1]$ the search moves j down to 1 and stops with the right message; if x is hit at some probe it stops with "x is in the array". It never prints a wrong message — the only failure is non-termination.

answer.value: The program loops forever whenever the range shrinks to $j=i+1$ with $a[i]<x$ (then $k=i$ and i := k makes no progress). This happens whenever $x>a[1]$ and x is not hit at a probe — i.e. x is absent and greater than $a[1]$, or x = a[N] (> a[1]); e.g. a = (1, 2), x = 2. Fix: use i := k+1.

pitfalls: The program never gives a wrong answer; it fails by not terminating.
cse-1996-b-66.verification: a = (1, 2, 3, 4): x = 3 is found at the second probe; x = 4 gets stuck at i = 3, j = 4, matching the rule.

cse-1996-b-67.approach: By reference, a is an alias of b, so every write to either is seen by both. By value-result, a is a local copy of b that is written back to b only on return.

steps.title: Call by reference
steps.body: b := 3; a ≡ b. a := 5 makes b = 5 → **point 1: 5 5**. test2 sets b = 10, so a = 10 → **point 2: 10 10**. After return **point3: 10**.

steps.title: Call by value-result
steps.body: a gets a copy 3. a := 5 (b still 3) → **point 1: 5 3**. test2 sets b = 10, a unchanged → **point 2: 5 10**. On return a (5) is copied back into b, overwriting 10 → **point3: 5**.

answer.value: (i) point 1: 5 5; point 2: 10 10; point3: 10. (ii) point 1: 5 3; point 2: 5 10; point3: 5.

pitfalls: With value-result the copy-back on return overwrites the 10 written by test2.
cse-1996-b-67.verification: The two modes differ only through aliasing: the change made by test2 is lost under value-result.

cse-1996-b-68.approach: An LR parser reduces bottom-up and left to right, so the print actions fire in post-order of the parse tree: each operand is printed before the operator that combines them — a postfix translation.

steps.title: Parse tree
steps.body: Root $E\to E*E$. Left child $E\to(E)$ with inside $E\to E+E$ over $E\to id(a)$, $E\to id(b)$; right child $E\to(E)$ with inside $E\to E+E$ over $id(c)$, $id(d)$.

steps.title: Reductions in order
steps.body:
1. $a\to E$: print **a**
2. $b\to E$: print **b**
3. $E+E\to E$: print **+**
4. $(E)\to E$: nothing
5. $c\to E$: **c**; 6. $d\to E$: **d**; 7. $E+E$: **+**; 8. $(E)$: nothing
9. $E*E\to E$: print \*

answer.value: Translation: a b + c d + * (postfix of (a+b)*(c+d)).

pitfalls: The rule $E\to(E)$ has no action, so parentheses never appear in the output.

cse-1996-b-69.approach: Trace which process reaches each join first: join N (N = 2) lets through only the second of the two arrivals (S1's and S2's processes), and join M (M = 2) only the second of S3's and S4's.

steps.title: Processes created
steps.body: fork L3 starts a process running S2 then goto L1; fork L4 starts one running S4 then goto L2. The parent runs S1 and falls into L1. So S1, S2, S4 run concurrently.

steps.title: join N at L1
steps.body: The parent (after S1) and the L3 process (after S2) both reach join N. The first decrements N to 1 and terminates; the second gets 0 and continues to S3. So **S1 → S3** and **S2 → S3**.

steps.title: join M at L2
steps.body: The process from S3 and the L4 process (after S4) meet at join M; the survivor runs S5. So **S3 → S5** and **S4 → S5**.

answer.value: Edges S1 → S3, S2 → S3, S3 → S5, S4 → S5 (S1, S2 and S4 have no predecessors and run concurrently).

cse-1996-b-69.verification: S5 can only run after both arrivals at join M, and one of them is after S3, which needs both S1 and S2.

cse-1996-b-70.approach: Compute Need = Max − Allocation and run the safety algorithm. For the request, pretend to grant it and run the safety check again.

steps.title: (a) Safety check
steps.body:
Work = (2, 2, 0).
- P1: Need (1, 2, 0) ≤ (2, 2, 0) ✓ → Work = (2, 2, 0) + (0, 3, 1) = (2, 5, 1).
- P0: Need (3, 1, 0) — 3 > 2 ✗; P2: Need (0, 2, 1) ≤ (2, 5, 1) ✓ → Work = (3, 5, 3).
- P0: (3, 1, 0) ≤ (3, 5, 3) ✓ → Work = (4, 5, 5).

Safe sequence **P1, P2, P0**, so the state is safe and the system can be in it (totals (4, 5, 5) cover every Max).

steps.title: (b) Pretend to grant (0, 1, 0) to P0
steps.body: Request ≤ Need (0,1,0) ≤ (3,1,0) ✓ and ≤ Available ✓. New Available = (2, 1, 0); P0 Allocation (1, 1, 2); P0 Need (3, 0, 0).

steps.title: (b) Safety check fails
steps.body: Work = (2, 1, 0): P0 needs 3 of R0 (> 2), P1 needs 2 of R1 (> 1), P2 needs 2 of R1 and 1 of R2 (> 1, > 0). No process can finish → **unsafe**. The request is not granted; P0 waits and the state is rolled back.

answer.value: (a) The state is safe: P1, P2, P0 can finish in that order. (b) Granting would leave the system unsafe, so the request is denied and P0 waits.

pitfalls: A request that fits in Available can still be refused — the test is safety, not availability.
cse-1996-b-70.verification: Total resources = Allocation sums + Available = (4, 5, 5) ≥ each process's Max.

cse-1996-b-71.approach: The number of files is limited by how many 32-bit directory entries fit in one 4 KB block; the file size is limited by how many data blocks an 8-bit FAT pointer can name.

steps.title: (a) Maximum number of files
steps.body: Directory = one block of $4\text{ KB}=4096$ bytes; entry = 32 bits = 4 bytes. $4096/4=1024$ entries → **1024 files**.

steps.title: (b) Maximum file size
steps.body: A FAT entry is 8 bits, so it can name at most $2^8=256$ different data blocks. (The 4 KB FAT block has room for 4096 entries, but only 256 blocks are addressable.) A single file can use at most all of them: **256 blocks** ($256\times4\text{ KB}=1\text{ MB}$).

steps.title: Remark
steps.body: If one 8-bit value is reserved as the end-of-chain / free marker, only 255 data blocks can be named, giving 255 blocks.

answer.value: (a) 1024 files; (b) 256 blocks (255 if one FAT value is reserved as the end-of-file marker).

pitfalls: The FAT block could hold 4096 one-byte entries, but 8-bit pointers limit the disk to 256 data blocks.

cse-1996-b-72.approach: Read the next-state equations off the circuit — a shift register $Q_1\to Q_2\to Q_3$ with $D_1=Q_2\oplus Q_3$ — and tabulate all 8 states.

steps.title: State diagram
steps.body:
$S_0$ has a self-loop. All other states form one cycle of length 7:
$$S_1\to S_4\to S_2\to S_5\to S_6\to S_7\to S_3\to S_1$$

answer.value: $S_0\to S_0$ (self-loop) and the 7-state cycle $S_1\to S_4\to S_2\to S_5\to S_6\to S_7\to S_3\to S_1$.

pitfalls: The state index uses $Q_1$ as the most significant bit: 100 is $S_4$.
cse-1996-b-72.verification: Each of the 8 states has exactly one successor and the 7-cycle plus the fixed point cover all 8.

cse-1996-b-73.approach: From the state table of Fig. 24 ($Q_1^+=Q_2\oplus Q_3$, $Q_2^+=Q_1$, $Q_3^+=Q_2$), follow the successors of $S_4$ until a state repeats.

steps.title: Unreachable set
steps.body: The walk visits 7 states. Only $S_0=000$ is missing; it maps to itself ($0\oplus0=0$), and no other state maps to it, so it can never be reached.

pitfalls: Starting from a non-zero state an XOR shift register never reaches all-zeros.
cse-1996-b-73.verification: The only predecessor of 000 is 000 itself (Q2 = Q1 = 0 and Q2 ⊕ Q3 = 0 force all zeros).

cse-1996-b-74.approach: Per block the CPU spends 1000 + 500 cycles; count blocks per second from the disk rate and compare with the 50 M cycles available per second.

steps.title: Blocks per second
steps.body: $\dfrac{2000\text{ KB/s}}{4\text{ KB/block}}=500$ blocks/s (one block every 2 ms).

steps.title: CPU cycles used
steps.body: Per block $1000+500=1500$ cycles; per second $500\times1500=750{,}000$ cycles.

answer.value: 1.5% of the processor time.

pitfalls: With DMA the CPU pays only the set-up and completion costs, not a cycle per byte.
cse-1996-b-74.verification: Per 2 ms block the CPU has $50\times10^6\times0.002=100{,}000$ cycles and uses 1500: 1.5%.

cse-1996-b-75.approach: Use the hierarchical model: every access pays level 1; a level-1 miss also pays level 2; a level-2 miss also pays level 3. $T=t_1+(1-h_1)\,[\,t_2+(1-h_2)\,t_3\,]$. Try the smallest level-1 size first.

steps.title: Choice
steps.body: The smallest (most expensive) cache, 8M, works only with the 64M main memory. So level 1 = **8M bytes**, level 2 = **64M bytes**, average **95 ns**.

steps.title: Caveat
steps.body: 16M cache with 4M main memory gives $50+0.1\times300=80$ ns with less total memory, and a model where each level's time is counted alone ($h_1t_1+(1-h_1)h_2t_2+\ldots$) makes 8M + 4M already reach 99.2 ns. The intended reading of "minimum sizes" is therefore uncertain.

answer.value: (a) Level 1 = 8M bytes, Level 2 = 64M bytes; (b) 95 ns (hierarchical model).

pitfalls: 16M main memory gives exactly 100 ns, which is not less than 100 ns.

cse-1996-b-76.approach: Read each query inside out: joins link users to their issued books, the selection filters, and the projection says what is reported.

steps.title: Query (a)
steps.body: $(USERS\bowtie ISSUED)\bowtie BOOKS$ pairs every issue record with its user and book. Projecting User#, BookTitle and then selecting User# = 6 leaves the titles of books issued to user 6.

steps.title: Query (b)
steps.body: $\sigma_{HomeTown=Delhi}(USERS\bowtie ISSUED)$ keeps issues made to users from Delhi; joining with BOOKS gives those books, and $\pi_{AuthorName}$ lists their authors.

answer.value: (a) The titles of all books issued to the user whose User# is 6. (b) The names of authors whose books have been issued to users whose home town is Delhi.

pitfalls: In (a) the selection after projection still works because User# is kept by the projection.
cse-1996-b-76.verification: Both queries only use attributes kept by their inner operations (User# in (a), AuthorName in (b)).
